summary: This work compares continuous coherent noise modeled as von Mises–Fisher distributed rotations on the Bloch sphere with discrete Pauli noise in quantum circuits, testing both on [[5,1,3]] and [[7,1,3]] stabilizer codes and Grover search algorithms. An entropy-matched comparison scheme and an approximate analytical method for propagating coherent errors through circuits are introduced, showing that continuous and Pauli noise produce comparable logical-error trends when syndrome extraction is applied.
motivation: Real quantum devices exhibit coherent gate errors from control drift and environmental coupling that accumulate with circuit depth, yet most error-correction approaches rely on discrete Pauli models. Understanding whether continuous coherent noise requires distinct treatment from stochastic Pauli faults is essential for accurate noise modeling and fault-tolerance thresholds.
method: Coherent errors are sampled as random rotations using an isotropic Gaussian distribution (small-angle limit of von Mises–Fisher with concentration $\kappa$, variance $\sigma^2 = 1/\kappa$). Fair comparison is enabled by matching continuous and Pauli channels via binary entropy $H$ at readout. An approximate propagation method tracks cumulative variances $v_{\theta,\phi}$ on each qubit without full Monte Carlo sampling, with updates $v_{\theta,\mathrm{new}} = v_\theta + \sigma^2$ per single-qubit gate and transparent CNOT propagation.
result: Continuous and Pauli noise yield comparable logical-error curves in stabilizer-code circuits after error correction (especially for [[5,1,3]]), consistent with syndrome extraction projecting general single-qubit errors onto Pauli subspaces. The approximation agrees with full simulations for uncoded circuits and random Clifford circuits (mean fidelity ratio $\approx 1.0$) but underestimates error in Grover search (non-Clifford), indicating the method's regime of validity is Clifford-dominated circuits.
